I would keep my land mainly in the local wheat-maize rotation, because that is the most reliable way for me to earn steady income in Quzhou County. The climate, irrigation conditions, buyers, and my own experience all fit winter wheat followed by summer maize better than taking big risks on niche crops. At the start of this season, I would continue managing the winter wheat already in the field, then switch that same land into summer maize right after harvest. I would use improved or hybrid seed rather than traditional seed because I want stable yield, stronger uniformity, and less uncertainty. For tillage, I would plough before wheat where I want a clean seedbed, then use rotary tillage for maize after wheat harvest so I can turn the field around quickly. On fertilizer, I would stay moderate rather than extreme: enough nitrogen for yield, with phosphorus and potassium to keep the soil from getting exhausted. I would irrigate wheat more often than maize because wheat here depends heavily on timely water at key stages, while maize can usually get by with fewer irrigations if the summer rains are decent. I would not spray on a fixed calendar just for the sake of spraying; I would keep applications limited, mainly for weeds and the main disease and insect pressure I usually face. My goal would be stable output and manageable costs, not chasing the absolute highest yield.
